title: Our nearest star system observed live
caption: The Southern Cross and Alpha and Beta Centauri over La Silla Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at La Silla Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The Southern Cross is easy to spot in the dark sky over ESO's La Silla Observatory, just right of the Danish 1.54-meter telescope's dome. Toward the lower right sparkle two stars, Alpha Centauri on the right and Beta Centauri on the left. Alpha Centauri, a multiple star, is the closest star system to Earth.

Its third member, Proxima Centauri, is too faint to see with the naked eye but is a little closer than the bright pair, just 4.2 light-years away, making it our nearest neighbor. Past observations offered faint hints that a small companion circles this red dwarf.

A campaign called the Pale Red Dot, which began in January 2016, set out to search more sensitively for the tiny wobbles in Proxima's motion that could reveal an Earth-like planet. The main tool was HARPS, the High Accuracy Radial velocity Planet Searcher on ESO's 3.6-meter telescope at La Silla.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph at ESO's La Silla Observatory, in visible light. The camera settings and color processing are not published.
understand.eye: A camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the sky looks more crowded with stars than it would to someone standing at the observatory.

explore: HARPS measurements were complemented by the Las Cumbres Observatory Global Telescope Network and the BOOTES system. The campaign also invited the public to follow the observations as they came in, with blog posts by astronomers, engineers and science writers on planet-hunting and the lives of stars.
alt: A telescope dome under a dark, starry sky, with a cross-shaped group of stars beside it and two bright stars at lower right.
